I think the idea of "market manipulation" of "Limiting 6800 supply" is looking at it the wrong way - unless they have a warehouse somewhere of navi21 dies that fail validation for higher-tier SKUs, isn't it obvious you'd sell the dies at the highest SKU they can, and they certainly seem to be selling all they can produce right now. Cutting down otherwise working dies to the 6800 spec would mean they get less money for perfectly working silicon, and would cause a lower supply of the higher tier SKUs.

I think what's more likely is they set the MSRP scale between the 6800/6800xt/6900xt based on expected yields of what navi21 dies can actually work at each SKU. But now, the yield is better than expected - so proportionally more of the dies meet the 6800xt and 6900 spec. And until they have saturated the market at those tiers (IE they're producing more than they're selling so they're just piling up sat on shelves), and they've already reduced the selling price to the lowest they're willing to go on that SKU would they cut down otherwise working dies to serve the lower market segments.

No "manipulation" needed, no "conspiracy", just AMD selling their dies at the best SKU spec each die is capable of.

text:
Not making 6800 cards isn't manipulating the market towards higher pricing for Navi 21 chips.  

If they did make more 6800 cards, that would be manipulating the market towards lower pricing, because they'd be cutting down working dies to fill in a lower-tier segment.  As you are well aware, AMD is a for-profit company.  Chip companies only cut down working chips to fill a market segment when they can't sell those chips at the higher tier price, and it's better to get some return than no return.  Absent that situation (which certainly seems to be the case now), the only supply for the lower-tier products is going to be partially defective dies that actually can't be the higher-tier products.  Given TSMC's high yields, that's not going to be a very high number for Navi 21.

Same is true for nVidia, only they're far less likely to actually sacrifice higher-margin top-tier dies to fill a lower-tier market segment.

The only way these companies will sacrifice top-end chips to make lower-priced cards is if people stop buying the higher-priced cards.

text:
I think its a little bit different in how AMD sells its Navi 21 SKU's.
-The RX6800 is a typical salvage SKU. The difference is that every RX6800 has one Shader Engine disabled. Basically chips that have some part of one Shader Engine not functioning, get sold like that. That is for example also why the RX6800 only has 96 ROPS and not 128.
-The RX6800XT is a mostly functional Navi 21 chip where one or a few CUs are not functioning up to standard, if at all. That leads to eight CU's being disabled. 
-The RX6900XT is a fully functional Navi 21 chip that AMD sells for a serious premium.
-The RX6950XT is again a fully functional Navi 21 chip that AMD sells for an even larger premium. 

What I think is happening here is that a combination of good yields and lower demand that makes the RX6900XT and RX6950XT more readily available. But instead of lowering the prices to satisfy more customer demand, they increased the price of the RX6900XT by giving it faster memory. This move basically makes the RX6900XT obsolete and I suspect those will no longer be produced. Thus you are looking at a price increase for a few percent faster. Meanwhile this does nothing for people who consider the "traditional" $600-700 range as their max for a high end video card.
